documents: Korrat et al. 2022, Pure Appl. Geophys. 179, 599–618 (published PDF)

entry.evidence: Following the approach of Ataeva et al. (9), the average values of the corner frequency ratio fc(P)/fc(S) and Mo vs. fc

steps.action: The authors pose the monitoring problem of telling small earthquakes from quarry blasts in data from the Egyptian National Seismological Network.
steps.quote: Distinguishing between small-magnitude events remains a challenging task.

steps.action: They take from Ataeva et al. (2017) the claim that the fc(P)/fc(S) ratio, and lower explosion corner frequencies in Mo vs. fc, separate quarry blasts from earthquakes.
steps.quote: the calculated ratios of P- to S-wave corner frequency fc(P)/fc(S) computed for each event have demonstrated significant segregation between earthquake and quarry blast groups

steps.action: They design the test: apply the Ataeva approach (Mo vs. fc and the fc(P)/fc(S) ratio) region by region in Northern, Central and Southern Egypt, and relate the ratio to Mw for the whole country.
steps.quote: Each region is checked individually to identify variations that can distinguish any of them.

steps.action: They select 440 earthquakes (depth < 25 km) and 450 quarry blasts with MD 1.5–3.3 from 2009–2015, recorded at three or more stations with SNR ≥ 10. Blasts are labelled from quarry reports independently of seismic means, and magnitudes and locations are matched between the two groups (§2 ¶2).
steps.quote: Most quarry blasts are identified from monthly reports of quarries received by the ENSN main center independently of seismic means.

steps.action: They compare earthquake and blast waveforms of equal magnitude at the same stations (Figs. 4 and 5), noting weak S-waves and Rg contamination in blast records.
steps.quote: It is evident that the displayed waveforms reveal the difference between an earthquake and an explosion

steps.action: They process the vertical-component records in EQK_SRC_PARA to obtain P- and S-wave displacement spectra: detrending, instrument deconvolution and conversion to velocity.
steps.quote: The source parameters for all events were investigated using the P- and S-wave displacement amplitude spectra obtained from the vertical component seismograms

steps.action: They test several P- and S-window durations to pick lengths (P 1.5–4 s, S 10–20 s) that avoid interference from other phases and give stable spectra.
steps.quote: Several checks with different durations of P- and S-waves were performed to select the optimum signal window length

steps.action: They correct the spectra for geometrical spreading (1/R), regional frequency-dependent QS, an assumed QP = 2QS, and kappa taken from prior Egyptian studies.
steps.quote: Adopting the above results, we assume the relation QP(f) = 2QS(f) for the frequency-dependent P-wave quality factor in this study.

steps.action: They show spectra before and after attenuation correction (Figure 6), reporting that the correction shifts the low-frequency level and, for small events, the corner frequency.
steps.quote: Figure 6 illustrates the effect of attenuation correction on displacement spectra

steps.action: They fit Brune's omega-square model by nonlinear least squares to estimate Ω0 and fc, compute Mo and Mw, and average these over stations as log means with standard deviations (Archuleta et al. 1982).
steps.quote: the nonlinear least-square inversion technique was performed to fit Brune's source model using EQK_SRC_PARA software

steps.action: They check the inter-station standard deviations of log fc, Mo and Mw (Table 2, Fig. 9) and judge them small enough for the discrimination analysis.
steps.quote: The average standard deviations values σ of corner frequency estimations were acceptable and practically validated for both earthquakes and explosions

steps.action: They compare Mo vs. fc (Fig. 10) and fc histograms (Fig. 11) for earthquakes and blasts. Blasts have lower fc, more clearly for S, and the overlap is 11.7%/1.25% (P/S) in the North and 18%/0.06% in Central Egypt.
steps.quote: explosions show markedly lower corner frequencies fc than earthquakes, particularly for S-wave displacement spectra

steps.action: They repeat the comparison across the three independent regional event sets. Southern Egypt shows complete separation and the other two show slight overlap.
steps.quote: In contrast, the Southern Egypt region observed a strong complete distinction between corner frequency values of earthquakes and explosions.

steps.action: They restate the expectation from Ataeva et al. that the fc(P)/fc(S) ratio is higher for explosions than for earthquakes.
steps.quote: Ataeva et al. (9) showed that the average ratio fc(P)/fc(S) is higher for explosions than earthquakes.

steps.action: They fit fc(P) against fc(S) per region (Fig. 12, Table 4). Earthquake ratios are 1.26–1.28 and blast ratios 1.86–2.0, matching the expected ordering.
steps.quote: the average fc(P) is larger than the average fc(S) for both events, but the average ratio fc(P)/fc(S) is larger for explosions

steps.action: They plot the ratio against Mw for all of Egypt (Fig. 13), find it independent of Mw, and set an empirical threshold of about 1.51–1.52 between the highest earthquake ratio and the lowest blast ratio.
steps.quote: The empirical threshold value is derived by averaging the highest earthquake ratio fc(P)/fc(S) and the lowest explosion ratio fc(P)/fc(S).

steps.action: They set the lower blast corner frequencies, steeper spectral fall-off and P/S discriminant beside published quarry-blast and nuclear-monitoring studies (§4 ¶3–¶4).
steps.quote: Many researchers also observed similar findings in quarry blast spectra

steps.action: They attribute the incomplete separation in the Northern and Central regions to near-surface geology and blasting practice (ripple-firing delay, hole layout), without testing either.
steps.quote: However, the variation in Mo vs. fc among the three Egyptian regions could be attributed to various near-surface geologies, particularly in explosion-prone areas.

steps.action: They compare the Egyptian ratios with Ataev et al. (2015, 2017) for Israel and Lebanon: earthquake ratios are slightly higher, and blast ratios match the North but are higher elsewhere.
steps.quote: This ratio is slightly higher than the values estimated by Ataev et al. (8, 9) in Israel and Lebanon.

steps.action: They attribute the differences from the Israel and Lebanon values to regional geology and propagation-medium properties, and the scatter in blast ratios to ripple-fire delay, local geology and fc ambiguity.
steps.quote: [...] likely because of regional differences in geological conditions and material properties of the propagation medium of each region

steps.action: They keep the fc(P)/fc(S) ratio as an Mw-independent discriminant for Egypt with a threshold of 1.51–1.52.
steps.quote: The fc(P)/fc(S) ratio is considered an effective discriminant for separating earthquakes and explosions in Egypt as it is unaffected by the moment magnitude Mw.

end.claim: For Egyptian events of MD 1.5–3.3 (Mw about 1.5–3.3), the fc(P)/fc(S) ratio is independent of Mw and separates quarry blasts (1.52–2.84) from earthquakes (1.04–1.51), with an empirical threshold of about 1.51–1.52.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the attenuation-corrected Brune-model fits that yield station-averaged P- and S-wave corner frequencies for every event, neither discriminant nor the threshold would exist.

gates.evidence: Action: the Ataeva et al. discriminant chose which parameters to compute (§1 ¶4), but the events came from an existing network archive (§2 ¶1). Claim: the expected ordering of fc and of the ratio could have failed, and overlap is reported for the Northern and Central regions (§3.2.1 ¶2). However, the threshold is derived in-sample from the extreme ratios (§3.2.2 ¶1) and is not tested on held-out events. Registration: no threshold or analysis plan is stated as fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Fast Fourier transform to obtain displacement spectra
Cumulative trapezoidal numerical integration of velocity to displacement
Nonlinear least-squares inversion for spectral parameters
Monthly quarry blasting reports used as ground-truth event labels

limits:
No review file, open discussion or earlier version was supplied. The paper was revised (Received June 2021, revised January 2022) and the acknowledgements thank two reviewers, but what changed is unknown, so no review sequence is coded. The supplement (additional waveforms and spectra) was not supplied.

The threshold (1.51–1.52) is set in-sample from the highest earthquake and lowest blast ratios, and no held-out events test it.

Inference: the reported dispersions sit oddly with Fig. 13 and §3.2.2 ¶1. Earthquake ratio σ of 0.41–0.63 (Table 4) would imply many earthquake ratios above 1.51, against the stated range 1.04–1.51, so σ may describe the fit of the fc(P)/fc(S) regression rather than the ratio itself. An S-wave overlap of 0.06% for Central Egypt, with roughly 70 events there, cannot be a fraction of events.

Inference: blast S windows are said to contain Rg energy (§3.1 ¶2), which could bias fc(S) low and inflate the blast ratio. This possible artifact is not tested as a rival. The regional differences are attributed to geology and ripple-firing practice (§4 ¶5–¶6) without any test. The labelling basis for blasts not covered by the quarry reports ("Most") is not stated. Mixed short-period and broadband instruments are not checked for their effect.

Sub-claims: the Mo vs. fc discriminant (lower blast fc, clearer for S-waves) is regularity_in_range with region-dependent overlap. Complete separation in Southern Egypt is regularity_in_range.

Alternative readings: the entry could be coded problem (§1 ¶1) rather than challenged_result. The composition could be natures_repetition rather than independent_replication.

disagreements.support: The Northern Egypt blast ratio matches Ataeva et al., while the Central and Southern ratios (1.86–2.0) are slightly higher.
disagreements.quote: The ratio computed by Ataeva et al. (9) matches those of the Northern Egyptian region, while the other two regions yield [...] .

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Several other P- and S-window durations
alternatives_considered.reason: Avoid interference from other phases and ensure stable spectra; the long S window is optimal per Ataeva et al.

No QP relationship exists for Egypt; the published relations give similar results

alternatives_considered.reason: The correction is needed for a reliable corner frequency and seismic moment
